scenes.narration: Before writing code, write the plan. Our expense tracker must add an expense, list the expenses, show totals by category, and save everything in a file. First decide what one expense looks like. It has a day, a category, an amount and an optional note. A dataclass is perfect for that. Then decide the actions, each as a small function. Finally, decide the rules. For example, an amount must be positive. Think of a blueprint before building a house. Walls, doors and wiring are decided on paper first.

For now, a plain number. We improve money in the next episode. [HL 8] An optional note. [HL 10] All expenses live in one list. [HL 12] Add expense builds an Expense, [HL 13] and appends it to the list. [HL 15] Lunch. [HL 16] A bus pass. [HL 17] And another food expense. [HL 18] Three expenses. code.source:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Expense:
    day: str
    category: str
    amount: float
    note: str = ""

expenses = []

def add_expense(day, category, amount, note=""):
    expenses.append(Expense(day, category, amount, note))

add_expense("2025-03-01", "food", 120.5, "lunch")
add_expense("2025-03-02", "travel", 60, "bus pass")
add_expense("2025-03-03", "food", 80)
print(len(expenses))
print(expenses[0])

scenes.narration: Here is the plan on one page. In the middle sits one list of Expense cards. Around it, four actions. Add puts a new card in the list. List shows the cards. Summary adds the amounts by category. Save writes the cards to a file, and loads them back at the start. Each action is a small function. If every function does one job, the project stays easy to change.

[HL 11] And the grand total. Two sixty point five.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: negative amounts are accepted
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We add a travel expense of minus five hundred. Nothing stops it, and the total becomes minus four hundred. No error, just a wrong answer. Validate at the door. If the amount is zero or less, raise a value error, and let the caller decide what to do.

shorts.title: Plan first
shorts.script: Before you type, plan. Our expense tracker must add, list, summarise and save. Write those four actions down, each as one small function. A plan on paper takes five minutes, and saves hours of rewriting later. Try it in your own file and watch what happens. Pause the video and type it out yourself. Say it out loud once. Then you remember it. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Plan before you type.

shorts.title: One expense
shorts.script: What does one expense look like? A day, a category, an amount, and a note. That is a perfect dataclass. Three lines of fields, and Python writes init, repr and eq for you. One small class, the heart of the project. Pause the video and type it out yourself. Say it out loud once. Then you remember it. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Model one thing.

shorts.title: Totals
shorts.hook: "To total by category, use a dictionary."
shorts.script: To total by category, use a dictionary. Loop over the expenses. For each one, get the total so far, or zero, and add the amount. Sort the keys when printing, so the order is steady every time. Say it out loud once. Then you remember it. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Try it in your own file and watch what happens. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Group with a dict.

shorts.title: Validate
shorts.script: A bug hides in many projects. Nothing stops a negative amount, and the total silently goes wrong. Check at the door. If the amount is zero or less, raise a value error. One check, in one place, protects everything. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Try it in your own file and watch what happens. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Validate at the door.
